title: Highway materials
summary: The aggregate test limits and the bitumen test conditions are the examinable content, and they must be exact because the options are close together. Two conceptual points earn marks repeatedly: flakiness is defined on the LEAST dimension at 0.6 of the mean while elongation is on the GREATEST at 1.8, and a higher softening point means a HARDER, less temperature-susceptible binder. Understand why a flaky aggregate that passes every strength test can still fail in the road, because that reasoning is what the shape limits exist to prevent.

sections.heading: Subgrade soil and its testing
sections.body:
**The subgrade is the foundation of the pavement**, and its strength governs the whole design of a flexible pavement.

**California Bearing Ratio (CBR)** — the standard measure:

> **CBR = (load to cause a given penetration in the soil) / (load for the same penetration in standard crushed stone) × 100%**

| Detail | Value |
|---|---|
| **Plunger diameter** | **50 mm** |
| **Rate of penetration** | **1.25 mm/min** |
| **Penetrations recorded at** | **2.5 mm and 5.0 mm** |
| Mould | 150 mm diameter, 175 mm high |
| Surcharge | 2.5 kg annular weights (simulating pavement weight) |
| **Soaking for design** | **4 days (96 hours)** |

**The rule for which value to take** is examined directly:

> Take the **2.5 mm value** normally. **If the 5.0 mm value is HIGHER, REPEAT the test** — and if it repeats, **use the 5.0 mm value**.

The reason for repeating is that a higher 5 mm value is anomalous (the curve should flatten, not steepen) and usually indicates a **surface irregularity or a stone under the plunger** — so the test is suspect. Only if it reproduces is the higher value genuine.

**Why soaked for 4 days:** the design must reflect the **worst condition the subgrade will experience**, which is saturation during and after the monsoon. Testing at the as-compacted moisture content would give a flattering result and an under-designed pavement. In Nepal, with an intense monsoon, the soaked value is the only defensible design basis.

**Typical CBR values:**

| Soil | CBR |
|---|---|
| **Highly plastic clay** | **2 – 5%** |
| Silty clay | 4 – 8% |
| Silt | 5 – 10% |
| Sandy soil | 10 – 25% |
| **Well graded gravel** | **40 – 80%** |
| Crushed stone | 100% (by definition) |

**Design CBR** is taken as the value exceeded by a stated percentage of test results — commonly the **90th percentile** for a major road (that is, 90% of results exceed it), which is a conservative choice reflecting the fact that the pavement fails where the subgrade is weakest.

**Other subgrade tests:**

| Test | Measures |
|---|---|
| **Modulus of subgrade reaction k** | **Plate load test**; the parameter used for **RIGID** pavement design |
| **Resilient modulus M_r** | Repeated load triaxial; used in mechanistic design |
| **Plate bearing test** | Load–settlement of a 750 mm plate |
| **Compaction (Proctor)** | OMC and maximum dry density |
| Atterberg limits, grading | Classification and frost susceptibility |
| **Field density** (core cutter, sand replacement) | Compaction control |

**The parameter distinction is worth fixing:**

> **Flexible pavement design uses CBR.**
> **Rigid pavement design uses the modulus of subgrade reaction k.**

They are not interchangeable, and the reason is the mechanism: a flexible pavement transmits load **grain to grain to the subgrade**, whose **shear strength** (CBR) therefore matters; a rigid slab **bridges** the subgrade, which acts as a **bed of springs** whose **stiffness** (k) matters.

**Subgrade requirements:** compacted to at least **97% of modified Proctor MDD** (100% for the top 500 mm on a major road), free of **organic matter and expansive clay**, adequately **drained** (the water table kept at least 0.6–1.0 m below the formation), and **stable in the soaked condition**.

**Problem subgrades and their treatment:**

| Problem | Treatment |
|---|---|
| **Expansive (black cotton) clay** | Remove and replace, or **lime stabilisation**, or a thick granular capping; **moisture control** is essential |
| **Soft clay / high water table** | Sub-surface drainage, a granular capping layer, geotextile separation |
| **Weak subgrade generally** | **Stabilisation** — lime (for clays), cement (for granular and silty soils), bitumen (for sands) |
| Frost-susceptible silt | Remove; provide a non-frost-susceptible sub-base |

**Stabilisation choice follows the soil**, and the pairing is examinable: **LIME for clays** (it reacts with the clay minerals, reducing plasticity and increasing strength), **CEMENT for granular and low-plasticity soils** (it cements the particles), and **BITUMEN for sands** (it binds and waterproofs). Using cement on a highly plastic clay fails, because the cement cannot mix intimately with the clay lumps.

sections.heading: Aggregates
sections.body:
**Requirements of a road aggregate**: **strength**, **hardness (resistance to abrasion)**, **toughness (resistance to impact)**, **durability (resistance to weathering)**, **good SHAPE**, **adhesion with bitumen**, and low **water absorption**.

**The tests and their limits** — these must be exact:

| Test | Measures | Limit for **wearing surfaces** | Limit for **other** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Aggregate impact value** | Resistance to **sudden shock** | **30%** | **45%** |
| **Aggregate crushing value** | Resistance to **gradually applied load** | **30%** | **45%** |
| **Los Angeles abrasion value** | Resistance to **wear (abrasion)** | **30%** | **50%** |
| **Flakiness index** | **Shape** | **25%** (15% for some surfacings) | 25% |
| **Elongation index** | **Shape** | **15%** | 15% |
| **Soundness** (Na₂SO₄ / MgSO₄) | Resistance to **weathering** | **12% / 18%** | — |
| **Water absorption** | Porosity | **≤ 2%** (0.6% preferred) | — |
| **Stripping value** | Bitumen adhesion in water | ≤ 25% | — |
| Polished stone value | Skid resistance retention | ≥ 55 for surfacing | — |
| Specific gravity | Quality | 2.6 – 2.9 | — |

**Both 30% and 45% are genuine limits**, and a question specifying a **wearing surface** requires **30%**. A candidate who has memorised only "45%" answers wrongly. The wearing surface takes the stricter limit because it is **directly exposed to wheel impact, braking and abrasion**, with no covering layer to distribute the load.

**Impact and crushing carry the same numerical limits but are not interchangeable** — an aggregate can be strong under a slowly applied load yet **brittle under impact**. The **impact test** was developed as the field alternative, being quicker and needing no compression machine. For **weak** aggregates the **10% fines value** is preferred, because the crushing value becomes unreliable when the material crushes progressively rather than at a definable load.

**Shape — the definitions, which must be exact:**

> **FLAKINESS index**: the percentage by weight of particles whose **LEAST dimension is LESS than 0.6 × the mean** dimension
> **ELONGATION index**: the percentage whose **GREATEST dimension EXCEEDS 1.8 × the mean** dimension

So **0.6 goes with the LEAST dimension** and **1.8 with the GREATEST** — and the two are always taught together precisely so that a question can offer 1.8 as a distractor for flakiness. Measured by a **thickness gauge** (slotted, for flakiness) and a **length gauge** (for elongation).

**Why shape matters as much as strength** — and this reasoning is worth carrying:

| Problem with flaky or elongated particles | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **They BREAK under compaction and traffic** | The **gradation changes after laying**; fines are generated |
| **Poor interlock** | They lie flat and slide over one another instead of keying |
| **Higher voids** | More binder or cement needed for the same result |
| Reduced workability in concrete | Higher water demand, hence lower strength |
| Weak planes | Lower crushing and impact resistance |

**The first is the most serious, and it is the point:** an aggregate that satisfies **every strength test in the laboratory** can still **fail in the road**, because the flaky particles **fracture during rolling** and the compacted layer then has a quite different gradation from the one designed. The strength tests are performed on the aggregate as delivered; the shape limits protect against what happens to it afterwards.

**The preferred shape is CUBICAL and ANGULAR** — angular for **interlock**, cubical so it **does not break**. The shape descriptors are **rounded, irregular, angular, flaky, elongated, and flaky-and-elongated**; rounded river gravel gives good workability but poor interlock, and flaky or elongated particles are undesirable in every application.

**Gradation:**

| Type | Character | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Well graded (dense)** | A full range of sizes; smaller fill the voids between larger | **Dense bituminous mixes, base courses** — high strength, low voids |
| **Uniformly graded (single size)** | Narrow range | Drainage layers, surface dressing chippings |
| **Gap graded** | Intermediate sizes deliberately omitted | Some special mixes |
| **Open graded** | Few fines, high voids | **Drainage layers, porous friction courses** |

**Fuller's curve** gives the maximum-density gradation:

> **p = 100 (d/D)^{0.5}**

and the **0.45 power curve** (with the exponent 0.45 instead of 0.5) is the modern maximum-density line used in Superpave mix design.

**Why a well-graded aggregate is stronger**: the smaller particles fill the voids between the larger, so there are **fewer voids to fill with binder**, and the particles **bear on one another** rather than floating in binder. That means **less binder for the same result**, hence lower cost and higher stability.

**Stripping** is the loss of adhesion between bitumen and aggregate in the presence of water:

| Aggregate type | Adhesion |
|---|---|
| **Acidic / siliceous** (quartzite, granite, sandstone) | **Hydrophilic — POOR adhesion**; water displaces the bitumen |
| **Basic** (limestone, basalt, dolomite) | **Hydrophobic — GOOD adhesion** |

Countered by **anti-stripping agents**, **hydrated lime or cement as filler**, and — most importantly — ensuring the aggregate is **DRY** when coated. Coating a damp aggregate guarantees stripping, whatever the additive.

This matters in Nepal because much of the available aggregate is **siliceous river material**, and the monsoon guarantees water in the pavement — so the stripping value test and the use of lime filler are not optional refinements.

sections.heading: Bitumen and bituminous materials
sections.body:
**The three related materials**, distinguished by origin — a standard question:

| Material | Origin |
|---|---|
| **Bitumen** | A **petroleum residue** from the distillation of crude oil; soluble in **carbon disulphide** |
| **Tar** | From the **destructive distillation of COAL or wood**; contains **free carbon**, more temperature-susceptible, less durable, and now largely superseded |
| **Asphalt** | A **mixture of bitumen with inert MINERAL matter** — natural asphalt, or mastic asphalt for flooring and waterproofing |

Note the American usage differs: in the USA "asphalt" means what elsewhere is called bitumen, which is a genuine source of confusion in the literature.

**The bitumen tests** — each measures a distinct property, and the conditions must be exact:

| Test | Measures | Conditions | Typical / limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Penetration** | **Consistency / hardness** | Needle, **100 g, 5 s, 25 °C** | Result in **units of 0.1 mm** |
| **Ductility** | Ability to **stretch without breaking** | Briquette pulled at **50 mm/min, 27 °C** | **Minimum 50 cm** for paving grades |
| **Softening point** | **Temperature susceptibility** | **RING AND BALL**, 3.5 g steel ball, water/glycerine bath heated at **5 °C/min**, ball falls **25 mm** | **35 – 70 °C** by grade |
| **Float test** | Consistency of **HARD** bitumen, too stiff for penetration | Float in a water bath | — |
| **Viscosity** | Flow resistance | At **60 °C and 135 °C** | The basis of viscosity grading |
| **Flash and fire point** | **SAFETY in heating** | Pensky-Martens closed cup | Flash **≥ 175 °C** |
| **Loss on heating** | Volatiles present | 163 °C for 5 h | ≤ 1% |
| Specific gravity | Quality control | 27 °C | 0.97 – 1.02 |
| Solubility in trichloroethylene | Purity | — | ≥ 99% |

**The softening point relation is the key conceptual point:**

> A **HIGHER softening point** means a **HARDER, LESS temperature-susceptible** binder.

| Climate | Binder required |
|---|---|
| **HOT** | **HIGH** softening point — resists **bleeding and rutting** |
| **COLD** | **LOWER** softening point — stays flexible, resists **cracking** |

**Nepal spans both extremes within one road network** — the Terai reaches over 40 °C in summer while high-altitude roads freeze — which is why binder grade selection varies by region and is not a national default. A binder chosen for the Terai will crack in Mustang; one chosen for the mountains will rut in Birgunj.

**Bitumen has no sharp melting point** — it softens gradually — which is why the softening point is defined by a specific test condition rather than being a physical constant.

**Grading systems:**

| System | Basis | Grades |
|---|---|---|
| **Penetration grading** (older, IS 73:1992) | Penetration at 25 °C | 30/40, 60/70, 80/100 |
| **VISCOSITY grading** (current, IS 73:2013) | **Viscosity at 60 °C** | **VG-10, VG-20, VG-30, VG-40** |

**The move to viscosity grading is a genuine improvement**, and the reason is worth stating: **viscosity at 60 °C is measured near the maximum pavement temperature**, so it predicts **in-service performance** — rutting resistance in particular — far better than a needle penetration at 25 °C, which is a temperature the pavement rarely experiences under load. **VG-30** is the general-purpose grade for Indian and Nepali paving work; **VG-40** for heavy traffic and hot climates.

**Modified binders:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Polymer modified bitumen (PMB)** | Elastomer (SBS) or plastomer (EVA) added; **wider temperature range**, better rutting and fatigue resistance |
| **Crumb rubber modified bitumen (CRMB)** | Waste tyre rubber; similar benefits, uses a waste stream |
| Natural rubber modified | — |

Modified binders cost more and are justified on **heavily trafficked, high-stress or extreme-climate** sections — junctions, gradients, bus stops, and high-altitude roads.

**Cutback bitumen** — bitumen thinned with a volatile solvent for **cold application**:

| Type | Solvent | Curing |
|---|---|---|
| **RC — rapid curing** | Naphtha / petrol | Fast |
| **MC — medium curing** | **Kerosene** | Medium |
| **SC — slow curing** | Diesel / light oil | Slow |

Used for **priming, patching and surface dressing in cold or wet conditions**, where hot bitumen cannot be applied. The solvent evaporates, leaving the bitumen — which means cutbacks release hydrocarbons and are increasingly replaced by emulsions for that reason.

**Bitumen emulsion** — bitumen dispersed as fine droplets in water with an **emulsifier**:

| Type | Setting |
|---|---|
| **RS — rapid setting** | Tack coats, surface dressing |
| **MS — medium setting** | Premix work |
| **SS — slow setting** | Prime coats, soil stabilisation, fine premix |

Also classified as **cationic** (positively charged droplets, adhering well to **siliceous** aggregate — hence generally preferred) or **anionic**.

**Emulsions are the preferred cold-application material** because they contain **water rather than a hydrocarbon solvent** — cheaper, safer and environmentally better — and they can be applied to a **damp** aggregate, which a cutback cannot. They **break** (the water separates and evaporates) leaving the bitumen film, and the colour change from **brown to black** is the visible sign that breaking is complete.

**Blown (oxidised) bitumen** is air-blown at high temperature, becoming **stiff and rubbery**; used for **roofing, pipe coating and joint filling** rather than paving.

**Plastic bitumen** — bitumen with a thinner and a filler — is used for **filling cracks** in masonry and pavements and for stopping leaks.

**Bituminous mix types**, from thin to thick:

| Mix | Character |
|---|---|
| **Surface dressing** | A **sprayed binder with a chipping cover**; a **waterproofing and skid-resistance treatment, NOT a structural layer** |
| **Premix carpet (open graded)** | 20 mm; a thin wearing course, usually with a seal coat |
| **Mix seal surfacing** | Similar, better graded |
| **Bituminous macadam (BM)** | Open graded base or binder course |
| **Dense bituminous macadam (DBM)** | **Dense graded binder course** — structural |
| **Bituminous concrete (BC) / asphalt concrete** | **Dense graded WEARING course** — the highest quality |
| **Semi-dense bituminous concrete (SDBC)** | Between BM and BC |
| Stone matrix asphalt (SMA) | Gap graded, fibre-stabilised; very durable wearing course |

**Surface dressing being non-structural is the point most often missed**: it seals and provides texture but adds no strength, so a structurally inadequate pavement is not improved by surface dressing — only protected from water while it continues to deteriorate.

**Marshall mix design** determines the **optimum binder content**:

| Property measured | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Stability** (load at failure, 60 °C) | **≥ 9 kN** typically |
| **Flow** (deformation at failure) | **2 – 4 mm** |
| **Air voids (Va)** | **3 – 5%**, design at **4%** |
| **VMA** (voids in mineral aggregate) | ≥ 13–15% by aggregate size |
| **VFB** (voids filled with bitumen) | 65 – 75% |

**The optimum binder content is chosen at 4% air voids**, subject to the stability and flow limits — and the reason 4% is targeted rather than zero is a genuine engineering balance:

| Too much binder | Too little binder |
|---|---|
| **Bleeding** (binder rises to the surface) | **Ravelling** (aggregate is not held) |
| **Rutting** (the mix is too plastic) | **Cracking** (brittle, no flexibility) |
| Loss of skid resistance | **Water ingress** and stripping |
| Aggregate floats rather than interlocking | Poor durability |

So the design walks a narrow line, and the **4% air void target** provides just enough space for the binder to expand into as it is compacted further by traffic — without leaving so much that water and air penetrate and age the binder.

formulas.label: California Bearing Ratio
formulas.expression: CBR = (test load / standard load) × 100%, at 2.5 mm and 5.0 mm penetration; plunger 50 mm at 1.25 mm/min
formulas.note: Take the 2.5 mm value; if the 5.0 mm is higher, REPEAT. Soak 4 days for design.

formulas.label: Design parameter by pavement type
formulas.expression: FLEXIBLE pavement → CBR (shear strength).   RIGID pavement → modulus of subgrade reaction k (stiffness).
formulas.note: Not interchangeable: flexible transmits grain to grain, rigid bridges on a bed of springs.

formulas.label: Aggregate strength limits
formulas.expression: impact and crushing: 30% wearing surfaces, 45% other.   Los Angeles abrasion: 30% / 50%.
formulas.note: Both figures are genuine. A question specifying a WEARING SURFACE requires 30%.

formulas.label: Shape indices
formulas.expression: FLAKINESS: least dimension < 0.6 × mean (limit 25%).   ELONGATION: greatest dimension > 1.8 × mean (limit 15%).
formulas.note: 0.6 with LEAST, 1.8 with GREATEST. Flaky particles BREAK under compaction, changing the gradation.

formulas.label: Bitumen test conditions
formulas.expression: penetration 100 g/5 s/25 °C ; ductility 50 mm/min at 27 °C, ≥ 50 cm ; softening point ring and ball, 5 °C/min, 25 mm fall
formulas.note: The float test is for HARD bitumen too stiff for penetration.

formulas.label: Softening point relation
formulas.expression: HIGHER softening point = HARDER, less temperature-susceptible binder
formulas.note: High for hot climates (resists rutting and bleeding), lower for cold (resists cracking).

formulas.label: Fuller's maximum density curve
formulas.expression: p = 100 (d/D)^{0.5} ;   modern 0.45 power line uses the exponent 0.45
formulas.note: A well-graded aggregate needs less binder, because small particles fill the voids between large ones.

formulas.label: Marshall mix design criteria
formulas.expression: design at 4% air voids ; stability ≥ 9 kN ; flow 2–4 mm ; VMA ≥ 13–15% ; VFB 65–75%
formulas.note: Too much binder gives bleeding and rutting; too little gives ravelling and cracking.

formulas.label: Soil stabilisation pairing
formulas.expression: LIME for clays ; CEMENT for granular and low-plasticity soils ; BITUMEN for sands
formulas.note: Cement on a highly plastic clay fails, because it cannot mix intimately with the clay lumps.
